patch.objective: Write and trace nested comprehensions, including flattening a list of lists
secondaryObjectives: Tell identity (is) from equality (==) and write polymorphic code that relies on shared behavior

sources.cite: Python Institute, PCAP-31-04 exam syllabus (revised November 2, 2026)
sources.note: Read 2026-11-17 through a summarizing fetch: Advanced Python Constructs and I/O 24%; 5.1.1 'Construct list, set, and dictionary comprehensions'. The case turns on tracing where a comprehension's expression is evaluated: inside it, once per row (a new list each time), or outside it, once (one list repeated); the identity test seats[0] is seats[1] tells them apart.

sources.cite: Python Institute, PCEP-30-03 exam syllabus (revised November 2, 2026)
sources.note: Read 2026-11-17 through a summarizing fetch: Section 03 Data Collections (26%) covers lists, including list membership with in and not in. The PCEP course's own objective names the shared-row trap of multiplying a nested list.

sources.cite: Python 3.15 documentation, Common Sequence Operations, note on s * n (not opened for this round)
sources.note: To verify: the standard library reference notes that items in s * n 'are not copied; they are referenced multiple times', with the [[]] * 3 example and the list comprehension fix. That page did not appear in a search for this round. Every behavior in the case follows from that rule: multiplying a list of one inner list repeats references to the same inner list.
